content: Dietary fiber refers to the indigestible components of plant-based foods that facilitate the movement of food through the digestive system, absorb water, and ease defecation. These fibers are primarily composed of non-starch polysaccharides, such as cellulose, as well as other plant-derived substances like dextrins, inulin, lignin, waxes, chitins, pectins, beta-glucans, and oligosaccharides. Classification of Dietary Fiber Dietary fibers are categorized based on their solubility in water. Insoluble Fiber Insoluble fiber is non-viscous and does not dissolve in water. It binds water, thereby reducing the transit time of food in the colon. Examples of insoluble fiber sources include the skin of plums, whole wheat, wheat and corn bran, flaxseed lignans, and vegetables like celery, green beans, and potato skins. Soluble Fiber Soluble fiber is viscous and undergoes fermentation in the large intestine, producing end-products with significant health benefits. Soluble fiber sources include oats, oat beta-glucan, psyllium (ispaghula), barley, soybeans, dried beans, peas, and citrus fruits. Soluble fiber has a greater impact on cholesterol absorption compared to insoluble fiber and may also aid in diabetes management. Fermentable Fiber The American Association of Cereal Chemists defines fermentable fiber as the edible parts of plants or similar carbohydrates that resist digestion and absorption in the small intestine but undergo complete or partial fermentation in the large intestine. This definition highlights that all plant parts we consume—such as skin, pulp, seeds, stems, leaves, and roots—contain fiber, both soluble and insoluble. Complex carbohydrates like starch, oligosaccharides, and polysaccharides are excellent sources of fiber. These fibers resist digestion in the stomach and small intestine, passing into the large intestine where they are either water-absorbing (insoluble) or water-dissolving (soluble). Fermentation in the colon by gut bacteria produces gases and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as butyric, acetic, propionic, and valeric acids, which have notable health benefits. Short-Chain Fatty Acids (SCFAs) SCFAs are absorbed through the colonic wall into the portal circulation, supplying the liver and entering the systemic circulation. They increase the acidity of the colon, which protects against colonic polyps and enhances the absorption of dietary minerals. SCFAs also stimulate the production of immune cells, antibodies, and cytokines, contributing to immune protection. Additionally, they promote the growth of beneficial colonic bacteria like Bifidobacteria and Lactobacilli, improve the barrier properties of the colonic mucosa, and inhibit inflammatory irritants. These effects collectively improve blood glucose and lipid levels, enhance colonic health, and regulate immune responses. Regulatory Guidance on Fiber Products North Americans consume less than 50% of the recommended dietary fiber intake, with youth consuming as little as 20%. This deficiency is linked to the obesity crisis in developed countries. Recognizing the health benefits of increased fiber intake, regulatory agencies like the FDA have approved health claims for fiber-rich food products. Clinical trials have demonstrated that fiber sources like psyllium seed husk and beta-glucan from oats and barley significantly reduce blood cholesterol levels, contributing to cardiovascular health and lowering the risk of certain cancers. Sources of Fiber The U.S. National Academy of Sciences recommends 20–35 grams of dietary fiber per day for adults, but the average American consumes only 12–18 grams daily. Fiber-rich foods include legumes, oats, rye, chia, barley, fruits (e.g., prunes, plums, berries), vegetables (e.g., broccoli, carrots), root vegetables (e.g., potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions), and psyllium seed husk. Insoluble fiber sources include whole grains, bran, nuts, seeds, and vegetables like green beans, cauliflower, zucchini, and celery. Fiber Supplements Soluble fiber supplements are widely available and may help manage gastrointestinal disorders, lower cholesterol, reduce colon cancer risk, and aid in weight loss. Prebiotic soluble fibers like inulin and oligosaccharides may alleviate symptoms of inflammatory bowel diseases such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis by producing SCFAs with anti-inflammatory effects. Psyllium husk, a bulk-forming laxative, is effective in reducing cholesterol levels and alleviating symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome, though it may cause bloating. Inulin Inulin, a type of oligosaccharide found in many plants, belongs to the fructan carbohydrate class. It is increasingly used in prepared foods due to its nutritional benefits. Inulin is subtly sweet and can replace sugar, fat, and flour in recipes. As a prebiotic fermentable fiber, it promotes the growth of beneficial gut bacteria and enhances the absorption of minerals like calcium, magnesium, and iron by upregulating mineral-transporting genes and proteins in the colon. Vegetable Gums Vegetable gum fiber supplements, such as guar gum and acacia gum, are effective for managing irritable bowel syndrome. These powders dissolve easily without an aftertaste and are relatively new to the market. Misconceptions About Fiber Contrary to popular belief, fiber does not bind to minerals and vitamins, nor does it restrict their absorption. In fact, fermentable fiber sources improve mineral absorption, particularly calcium. Reduced bioavailability of certain nutrients is primarily due to the food's phytate content, not fiber. Summary of Health Benefits High-fiber diets improve gastrointestinal health, enhance glucose tolerance and insulin response, reduce hyperlipidemia and hypertension, lower the risk of certain cancers, and promote satiety, aiding in weight management. The physiological effects of fiber depend on its type, and the benefits of high-fiber diets result from the combined effects of various fiber types and other dietary components.
